crosswalks.label: Software Developers
crosswalks.rationale: Software Developers provide the strongest broad occupational baseline for distributed software implementation, interface/integration and performance work, but do not isolate distributed protocol engineering.

crosswalks.label: Computer Network Architects
crosswalks.rationale: Network Architects describe topology, capacity and network behavior that distributed systems depend on, but network infrastructure remains adjacent ownership rather than part of the AXM profession identity.

findings.summary: O*NET occupational evidence supports software integration, performance and network-adjacent work relevant to distributed systems, while the protocol/fault-model specialization requires a narrower AXM boundary.
findings.rationale: The body narrows the broad software baseline into protocol invariants, fault models, retries, replication and recovery.

findings.summary: Distributed protocol assumptions must stay separate from network-infrastructure guarantees; transport topology, capacity and operational behavior require Network/SRE/Infrastructure evidence.
method_labels: O*NET Software Developer plus Network Architect crosswalk comparison
findings.rationale: The occupations overlap operationally but represent distinct work structures; collapsing them would let protocol machinery invent network guarantees.

gaps_against_body.description: Keep distributed protocol assumptions separate from network-infrastructure guarantees and require explicit network/SRE evidence for environment-dependent claims.

nonclaims: This packet does not claim complete reconstruction of Distributed Systems Engineer.
Software Developer and Network Architect mappings remain partial/adjacent rather than profession identity.
No broad fault-tolerance, production-readiness, capacity, TEST, WORKING or CANON claim is created by this research packet.

high_stakes.authorization_nonclaim: This packet grants no production fault-injection, network, SRE, infrastructure, product or institutional authority.
